summary: This experimental document describes Compressed Bundle Header Encoding, a convention for convergence-layer adapters to represent endpoint identifiers compactly in the primary block of DTN bundles. It works when the identifiers follow a prescribed structure.

eli5.summary: Long addresses can be shortened with a code when both ends follow the same pattern. That makes the parcel label smaller.

questions: how to shrink dtn endpoint ids
what is the ipn uri scheme
how does dtn header compression work
subtitle: A way to squeeze the four endpoint addresses in a DTN bundle header down to eight small numbers.

tldr.problem: A Bundle Protocol primary block carries up to four endpoint identifiers as text strings, so the header can be a large share of a bundle whose payload is small.
tldr.mechanism: If every endpoint ID is the null ID or an ipn-scheme URI of the form node.service, the convergence-layer adapter replaces the text dictionary with eight integers and sets the dictionary length to zero.
tldr.outcome: Headers get much shorter, but only between adapters that both understand CBHE. The RFC is Experimental, and RFC 9758 has since updated it.

today: RFC 6260 is an Experimental RFC from the Internet Research Task Force, and it has been updated by RFC 9758. It was published for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation.

sections.title: Why Compress Bundle Headers
sections.content:
In Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN), the Bundle Protocol (RFC 5050) moves data in bundles. Each bundle's primary block holds four endpoint identifiers (EIDs): source, destination, report-to and current custodian. Each EID is a URI made of a scheme name, a colon and a scheme-specific part.

The primary block already saves space. The strings go into a dictionary at the end of the block, and each EID is represented by a pair of offsets. Duplicate strings may be left out. Even so, the strings are still text, so the header can be a very large fraction of a bundle with a small payload, as is expected for uses such as space flight operations and for administrative records.

Compressed Bundle Header Encoding (CBHE) cuts this further. It is a convergence-layer adaptation, so it is opaque to bundle processing and does not affect interoperability between Bundle Protocol implementations. It only affects interoperability between convergence-layer adapter (CLA) implementations.
sections.eli5: A parcel label with four long text addresses is bulky. If the parcel is tiny, the label can be bigger than what is inside, so this RFC finds a shorter way to write the addresses.

sections.title: The ipn Scheme and CBHE-Conformant IDs
sections.content:
CBHE works only when every endpoint ID in the primary block is CBHE conformant. Two forms qualify: the null endpoint ID dtn:none, and any ID in the new ipn URI scheme. The RFC defines ipn because the syntax in use for the existing dtn scheme is unsuitable for CBHE's compression.

An ipn scheme-specific part is a node number (1 to 2^64 - 1), a period, and a service number (0 to 2^64 - 1). For example, ipn:9.37 is conformant. The service number acts like a demultiplexing token, similar to a protocol number in an IP packet or a port number in a UDP datagram.

Negative values and values above 2^64 - 1 are not allowed because they cannot be encoded into the Self-Delimiting Numeric Values (SDNVs) used for the offsets. Node number zero is reserved for the null endpoint, and decompressing it must always give back dtn:none.
sections.eli5: An ipn address is just two numbers with a dot between them, like a building number and a room number. Building zero means nobody.

sections.title: Dictionary Order Constraint
sections.content:
Turning integers back into a dictionary only works if the original dictionary had a known layout, because the Bundle Protocol does not require any particular string order or the omission of duplicates. So CBHE compression is allowed only if the dictionary is exactly the following strings, in this order and with nothing added:

  1. Destination scheme name.
  2. Destination scheme-specific part.
  3. Source scheme name and scheme-specific part, each only if different from any prior string.
  4. Report-to scheme name and scheme-specific part, each only if different from any prior string.
  5. Current custodian scheme name and scheme-specific part, each only if different from any prior string.

A bundle with extension blocks that hold EID references to endpoints other than the destination, source, report-to and current custodian cannot be CBHE compressed, since its dictionary would not match this structure.
sections.eli5: To rebuild the long labels from the short codes, the packing list has to be in a fixed order. If someone put extra items in the box, the trick will not work.

sections.title: Compressing and Decompressing
sections.content:
Compression happens in the sending CLA when it transmits the bundle. The eight SDNVs that normally hold scheme-name and SSP offsets instead hold eight integers: node and service number for the destination, then source, then report-to, then current custodian. Any endpoint that is the null endpoint is written as zero. The dictionary is omitted and the primary block's dictionary length is set to zero.

On reception, a CBHE-conformant CLA recognizes a dictionary length of zero (and only that), may infer that the sending CLA is CBHE conformant, and MUST decode the block before handing it to the bundle protocol agent. Decompression simply reverses the process and rebuilds the standard dictionary.

A CLA MAY compress only when the constraints are met and the receiver is known or presumed to be CBHE conformant. That knowledge can come from node administration or from having received a CBHE-compressed bundle. A non-conformant CLA that receives a bundle with dictionary length zero passes it on unchanged, and the bundle protocol agent cannot determine the destination, so the bundle is judged malformed.
sections.eli5: The sender swaps the long addresses for eight short numbers and leaves a note saying the long list is gone. The receiver sees the note and rebuilds the long addresses from the numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some security features stop compression. The Bundle Security Protocol (RFC 6257) can add endpoint ID strings to the dictionary and reference them from extension blocks. A bundle cannot be CBHE compressed in those cases, for example when the Bundle Authentication Block's security-source endpoint is noted in the dictionary.

The inference rule also opens a possible denial-of-service attack. Malicious code could send a CBHE-compressed bundle whose source EID falsely names a node whose CLA is not CBHE conformant. A receiver might then wrongly start compressing everything it sends to that node, and those bundles could not be dispatched. Nodes can defend by requiring Bundle Authentication Blocks and discarding the inference for nodes that send inauthentic bundles.

The IANA section registers ipn as a provisional URI scheme. Apart from these caveats, CBHE adds no security considerations beyond those of RFC 5050 and RFC 6257.
sections.eli5: A trickster could lie about who sent a parcel so that someone starts using short codes with a friend who cannot read them. Checking who really sent the parcel stops this.
